article.title: Z.ai's GLM-5.4 and Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Mini Converge on Looped Transformers Days Apart, With Different Designs
article.summary: Days apart, Z.ai and Thinking Machines each shipped a looped-transformer model that reuses layers instead of adding parameters, but reached the idea by different, unverified routes.
article.body_markdown:
## Background

A standard transformer processes each token through every layer of the network exactly once per forward pass. For years, labs seeking more reasoning capacity have mostly added more layers — more stored parameters — rather than reusing the ones a model already has. [VentureBeat reports](https://venturebeat.com/technology/z-ais-glm-5-4-aims-to-match-models-up-to-four-times-its-size-by-running-28-layers-twice) that researchers explored layer reuse as far back as the 2018 Universal Transformer, whose authors described their proposal as "a parallel-in-time self-attentive recurrent sequence model which can be cast as a generalization of the Transformer model and which addresses these issues," combining "the parallelizability and global receptive field of feed-forward sequence models like the Transformer with the recurrent inductive bias of RNNs," according to the [original paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.03819). [Thinking Machines Lab's own announcement](https://thinkingmachines.ai/news/inkling-2-mini/) likewise cites that 2018 paper as foundational prior work.

The idea resurfaced in deployment-cost research more recently. A 2025 paper on [Relaxed Recursive Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.20672), accepted at ICLR 2025, opens by noting: "Large language models (LLMs) are expensive to deploy. Parameter sharing offers a possible path towards reducing their size and cost, but its effectiveness in modern LLMs remains fairly limited." The paper's authors — none affiliated with either company discussed below — built small recursive models that matched or beat similarly sized conventional models on benchmarks, suggesting the technique could scale. The sources cited in this article do not describe an earlier large, production-scale model built this way; the two releases below are the first the Herald has found reported at that scale.

## Current situation

Three days apart in November 2026, two AI labs released large language models built on that same underlying idea — reusing some of a model's own layers more than once per token instead of stacking new ones — but arrived at it through different technical paths.

Thinking Machines Lab, the San Francisco startup led by former OpenAI chief technology officer Mira Murati, released Inkling 2 Mini the day before [VentureBeat's November 21, 2026 report](https://venturebeat.com/technology/thinking-machines-wows-with-inkling-2-mini-looped-transformer-model-that-runs-locally-on-laptops), putting the launch on November 20. Inkling 2 Mini is a 24-layer, decoder-only sparse Mixture-of-Experts model with 26.4 billion total parameters, according to both VentureBeat and [Thinking Machines' own announcement](https://thinkingmachines.ai/news/inkling-2-mini/). Of those layers, Thinking Machines says the model is "divided into four blocks of six layers each. The two middle blocks run three times, while the first and last blocks each run once," which the company says yields "48 layer applications per token from 24 stored layers." The design, Thinking Machines writes, "is motivated by the intuition that the middle layers of the model carry more abstract reasoning, while the first and last few layers devote more space to translating between embeddings and internal representations." According to VentureBeat, Thinking Machines built the compact model by pruning two-thirds of its experts mid-training and distilling from a larger internal Inkling model, then ran supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, and in its own internal scaling tests found that "a non-looping baseline required 140% more inference compute to match the looped model's loss on 512K-token agentic traces." Inkling 2 Mini shipped with full weights on Hugging Face under the Apache 2.0 license.

Z.ai made GLM-5.4 available the same day, according to [VentureBeat's November 23, 2026 report](https://venturebeat.com/technology/z-ais-glm-5-4-aims-to-match-models-up-to-four-times-its-size-by-running-28-layers-twice) — the company's first flagship built on what it calls a "Loop Transformer architecture, which reuses the same layers more than once instead of stacking new ones, so the model gets more depth and more computation per token without adding parameters." Z.ai took a different route than Thinking Machines: rather than training a new, smaller model, it adapted its existing GLM-5 base, where "GLM-5.4 loops 28 layers of the GLM-5 base for two iterations at the 750B scale, adapted from an already pre-trained model through continued training." Of the ultra-long-chain reasoning tasks it says it is targeting, Z.ai said: "Stacking parameters and memorizing data cannot solve this." To manage the cost of looping a model that size, VentureBeat reports Z.ai added three changes: "Gated progressive updates" use per-token gates to control how much each pass changes internal representations; a "Hybrid KV cache" reuses the first pass's sparse cache rather than building a full new one for the second pass; and "Sparse attention index reuse" reuses the first loop's attention indices to avoid a second indexing pass.

The two companies' public evidence for their approaches differs in scope. Z.ai's "main controlled evidence is a 30B test model, where the looped version used about 10% more training compute than a non-looped baseline of the same size," with reported gains "by about 15% on MMLU-Pro and 12% on GPQA-Diamond" — but, as VentureBeat notes: "Those results were measured on the smaller test model, not GLM-5.4 itself." Z.ai separately published a win-rate chart comparing GLM-5.4 to three other models, which VentureBeat says arrived "without explaining the evaluation methodology," and the company acknowledges, per VentureBeat, that the model can get stuck in overly long reasoning loops. Licensing also differs: Inkling 2 Mini is already open under Apache 2.0, while GLM-5.4 remains closed, with Z.ai stating only: "We plan to open-source the model weights responsibly after completing necessary safety hardening," with no date given. GLM-5.4 adds vision to the lineup — according to [Z.ai's own documentation](https://docs.z.ai/guides/llm/glm-5.4) and confirmed by VentureBeat, it accepts text, image, video and file inputs with a 1-million-token context window and a 128,000-token output cap, up from GLM-5.3's text-only input.

The Machine Herald has already covered Inkling 2 Mini from two other angles: a [comparison of its benchmark scores and pricing against Google's Gemini 4 Neon](/article/2026-11/22-gemini-4-neon-and-inkling-2-mini-claim-near-frontier-scores-at-lower-cost-but-both-trail-on-some-cited-benchmarks), and a [separate analysis](/article/2026-11/23-looped-transformers-test-a-2025-ai-safety-warning-on-chain-of-thought-monitoring-in-thinking-machines-inkling-2-mini) of Thinking Machines' own tests of whether looping weakens chain-of-thought safety monitoring. The sources cited in this article do not report Z.ai running or publishing any comparable monitorability testing for GLM-5.4.

## Implications

Two labs independently converged on the same core idea — adding computational depth by reusing layers rather than adding new ones — within three days of each other, but took different routes to get there. Thinking Machines built a new, deliberately compact model from a pruned and distilled internal predecessor, purpose-built to run outside the cloud on a laptop or single GPU. Z.ai instead retrofitted looping onto an already-trained, 750-billion-parameter frontier model through continued training. That divergence suggests there is not yet one accepted implementation of a looped transformer among the labs that have adopted the idea: Thinking Machines loops only its middle 12 of 24 layers, three times each, in a 26.4-billion-parameter model purpose-built for efficiency; Z.ai loops all 28 layers of a 750-billion-parameter model — roughly thirty times larger by parameter count, on the Herald's calculation — twice each, with additional caching and gating machinery layered on to manage the cost.

Neither company's efficiency claims are independently verified in the sources cited here. Z.ai's reported MMLU-Pro and GPQA-Diamond gains were measured on a 30-billion-parameter proxy model rather than on GLM-5.4 itself, and its win-rate comparison against three rival models did not disclose an evaluation methodology, according to VentureBeat. Thinking Machines' figure that a non-looping baseline needs 140% more inference compute to match Inkling 2 Mini's loss comes from the company's own internal scaling tests. None of the sources cited in this article report a third party independently reproducing either company's efficiency comparisons, or testing the two architectures head to head.

Both companies trace the underlying idea back to the 2018 Universal Transformer, and academic interest in layer and parameter sharing has continued since: the 2025 Relaxed Recursive Transformers paper found that sharing parameters across layers "offers a possible path towards reducing their size and cost, but its effectiveness in modern LLMs remains fairly limited" at the time it was written. That two separate labs have now each built a production-scale looped model within days of each other — at very different sizes, for different purposes, with different safeguards against the technique's own instability risks — indicates the approach has moved from a narrow research question toward active industry experimentation, even though the sources reviewed here do not show the field converging on a shared method for doing it, or on independent confirmation that either implementation delivers the gains its maker reports. Whether other labs follow, and whether GLM-5.4's weights are released on a timeline that would let outside researchers test Z.ai's version the way Inkling 2 Mini's Apache 2.0 release already allows for Thinking Machines', is not addressed in the sources cited here.
